accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE National Curriculum in England, science, Working scientifically for KS1 ('use their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions') and lower KS2 ('use results to draw simple conclusions, make predictions for new values, suggest improvements and raise further questions'), and NGSS K-2 practice 'Engaging in argument from evidence'. Floating facts checked against the Royal Society of Chemistry and BBC Bitesize KS1/KS2 floating and sinking guides: wood, cork and apples are less dense than water and float; solid stone, a coin and a steel key sink; the adult text notes that hollow metal boats float and that density, not size, decides. Falling balls of equal size landing together from a short drop matches Galileo-style classroom demonstrations (air resistance negligible). Cress germinating on damp cotton wool and cuttings rooting in water are standard KS1 activities (RHS School Gardening). Parameter answers n-k, s, n-s and a+b stay positive at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented confirmation-bias habits in children's reasoning (Kuhn 1989 'Children and adults as intuitive scientists'; Chinn & Brewer 1993 responses to anomalous data: ignoring, rejecting, excluding, reinterpreting): keeping an idea because most results fit (keep, most, one), rejecting data without a reason (blame, water, the 'cress is not a real plant' option), hiding data (hide), repeating a test until it agrees (redo, fit), trusting the crowd (crowd), the size-decides-floating idea itself (apple, log), flipping to the opposite idea without checking (flip), and the opposite slip of changing an idea after one odd result (rush), plus the belief that an idea is proved for ever (proved, never).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagrethink is about revising a claim against evidence: each result in the water tank must be judged against the stated idea, the learner chooses the scientist's next move in three dilemmas, picks a replacement idea that must fit all four logged results and then uses it to predict new objects before they drop, repeats the cycle with plant evidence by dragging cards to Fits / Does not fit, and sorts scientist habits. It differs from flagfair (fair-test variables), floating-and-sinking labs and the plant-needs labs; the gate reports under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the anomaly before being told: the big apple floats and the small coin sinks while the idea is on screen, and the board marks them ✗. The 'what next' choices then force the decision, wrong ideas are rejected with the specific result that breaks them (the round coin sank), and the chosen idea is tested by predicting the wooden spoon, metal key and big log before each drop, so the learner sees a better idea make correct predictions.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'It sinks' for the big apple (the stated idea predicts it; the apple floats), 'One that fits what you thought' teaching more (the step shows surprises drive every change), 'Cress is not a real plant' or 'one test is never enough' (the plant step rejects explaining away), and 'No, it means they were bad' for changing your mind (the habit sort marks it good science). The completion message echoes each locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with two wrong options each, every one with its own message: skip (every result counts), water (blaming the test needs a reason), rush (one odd result could be a slip), forget (never forget a surprise), hide, crowd, fail (a surprise is not a failure), fit (testing until it agrees is not fair), one and most (one or most is not all), proved and never (ideas fit the evidence so far and can change). In-lab wrong moves name the slip too, e.g. 'The coin is round, and it sank. This idea does not fit.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the learner limits; kid paragraphs are short sentences with concrete examples (rock, apple, cress), adult text within 9.5. Canvas prompts are single instructions ('Drop the apple in.', 'Does the coin fit the idea?'). The precise terms for the age are used consistently: idea, test, result, evidence, fits / does not fit, predict.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step has one job (judge results, decide the next move, replace and test the idea, transfer to plants, name good habits) and every feedback line gives the specific result or reason. Item explanations give the reason rather than restating the answer.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px in light and dark, before and after Show me for every step. After the first pass the evidence board was shortened to '✓ rock sank' / '✗ apple floated' with a key line, because the two-column 'does not fit' labels overlapped at 360 px. Option pads are full-width and about 48 px tall, the tank fills three quarters of the width, and every canvas action has a large button below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Everything is doable with buttons: 'Drop the apple in', 'Fits the idea' / 'Does not fit', each next-move option, each new idea, 'It will float' / 'It will sink', the plant piles and idea choices, and 'Good science' / 'Not good science'. The canvas aria-label states the scene after each move, e.g. 'The apple floated. Does it fit the idea?' or 'Card: I will test it again to check.'. Challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors.
